reference.source: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle / Apley and Solomon's System of Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: The tibialis posterior is the principal dynamic stabiliser of the medial longitudinal arch; it inverts the hindfoot and locks the transverse tarsal joint to create a rigid lever for push-off, so its failure produces a progressive collapsing flatfoot

It is the commonest cause of acquired adult flatfoot, classically in middle-aged women, and is associated with obesity, hypertension, diabetes, corticosteroid use and seronegative inflammatory arthropathy
Early disease causes medial hindfoot pain and swelling behind the medial malleolus; as the arch collapses, lateral subfibular impingement pain can develop
The too-many-toes sign and an inability to perform a single-limb heel raise with hindfoot inversion are key bedside tests of tendon competence

The Johnson and Strom staging, with the Myerson modification, runs from tenosynovitis with a flexible foot, through a flexible then rigid flatfoot, to fixed deformity with ankle valgus and deltoid ligament failure
A watershed zone of relative hypovascularity just distal and posterior to the medial malleolus predisposes the tendon to degeneration and rupture

Flexible deformity is managed with orthoses, medial arch support or an ankle-foot orthosis and structured rehabilitation, whereas fixed deformity or ankle involvement requires reconstructive or fusion surgery
reference.pathophysiology: Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction begins as degenerative tendinosis and tenosynovitis within the watershed hypovascular segment behind the medial malleolus, where repetitive load, ageing and impaired healing lead to mucoid degeneration, elongation and eventual attritional rupture. As the tibialis posterior loses its inverting and arch-supporting action, the unopposed peroneus brevis and the body's weight drive progressive hindfoot valgus, forefoot abduction and collapse of the medial longitudinal arch. Secondary attenuation of the spring (plantar calcaneonavicular) ligament and later the deltoid ligament allows the talar head to plantarflex and the deformity to become fixed, with lateral subfibular and sinus tarsi impingement and, in advanced disease, valgus tilt of the ankle. Inflammatory arthropathy and metabolic factors accelerate this degenerative cascade.
additionalDifferentials: Tarsal coalition or accessory navicular causing a rigid or painful flatfoot
Midfoot or hindfoot osteoarthritis and Charcot neuroarthropathy
Inflammatory arthropathy such as rheumatoid or seronegative spondyloarthritis
Deltoid or spring ligament injury without primary tendon disease
Tarsal tunnel syndrome or medial ankle nerve entrapment
Deep posterior compartment or medial ankle tenosynovitis of other tendons
additionalInvestigations: Weight-bearing foot and ankle radiographs assessing talonavicular coverage, talo-first metatarsal alignment and arch collapse
MRI to grade tendon degeneration, tears and associated spring and deltoid ligament involvement
Ultrasound for dynamic assessment of tendon integrity and tenosynovitis
Standing hindfoot alignment view or weight-bearing CT for coronal deformity
Single-limb heel-rise test and too-many-toes assessment documented over time
Screening for inflammatory arthropathy and metabolic risk factors where clinically indicated
redFlags: A hot, deformed insensate foot suggesting Charcot neuroarthropathy, especially in diabetes
Rapidly progressive deformity or fixed valgus with ankle involvement
Features of an inflammatory or septic process rather than degenerative tendinopathy
Neurovascular compromise or non-healing medial ankle ulceration
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis, flexible deformity often responds well to orthoses and rehabilitation, and joint-preserving reconstruction can restore function; once deformity becomes rigid or the ankle is involved, arthrodesis is usually required and full correction of established deformity is less predictable.
pitfalls: Dismissing early medial ankle pain and swelling as a simple sprain and missing tenosynovitis
Failing to distinguish a flexible from a rigid deformity, which fundamentally changes management
Overlooking a hot deformed neuropathic foot and treating Charcot arthropathy as tendon dysfunction
Attempting soft-tissue reconstruction alone without correcting hindfoot malalignment with osteotomy, so the reconstruction fails
references: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
Apley and Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Trauma
management: Manage early flexible disease non-operatively with medial-arch orthoses or a custom foot orthosis and immobilisation in a walking boot or cast during acute tenosynovitis
Prescribe eccentric tibialis posterior strengthening and calf-stretching physiotherapy, with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for pain, and avoid corticosteroid injection into the tendon
Address modifiable contributors including obesity, diabetes and inflammatory arthropathy
Offer joint-preserving reconstruction, such as flexor digitorum longus tendon transfer with a medialising calcaneal osteotomy, for flexible deformity failing conservative care
Perform hindfoot or triple arthrodesis for rigid, fixed deformity or when the ankle joint is involved
Monitor deformity progression with the single-limb heel-rise test, too-many-toes sign and weight-bearing radiographs
Refer to orthopaedic and podiatry services for staging-based decision-making
